headline: Zero-Cost Cloud Deployment for personal projects, 24/7 online
summary: Learn how to deploy your web apps to smartphones and keep them online 24/7 without recurring cloud invoices, leveraging generous free tiers.
details: This guide details the final installment of the LifeOps engineering series, focusing on achieving 24/7 cloud deployment and mobile optimization for personal projects without incurring costs. It demonstrates how to overcome the common obstacle of complex production deployment and costly app store fees by utilizing the most generous free tiers available.

To ensure LifeOps remains online 24/7 on Render's free tier, the strategy involves leveraging its free offerings. While the tier includes container hibernation after 15 minutes of inactivity, the application handles this by providing an informative, guided user experience for initial loads, mitigating potential gateway timeouts.

Mobile optimization is addressed by configuring Rollup manual chunking for sub-second initial loads across 4G and 5G networks. Stable external dependencies like vendor-react and @supabase are cached by user browsers, ensuring that only lightweight diffs of new business logic are downloaded when features update.

The mobile user experience is anchored on three ergonomic pillars: a fixed footer navigation with large touch targets, a responsive sidebar that adapts to screen size, and modals that remain accessible regardless of form length, ensuring thumb-friendly interaction.

To achieve a native mobile feel without store middlemen, modern meta tags and web app standards are configured in index.html. This allows applications to be installed directly from the browser, bypassing the usual store gatekeepers and associated fees.

The core takeaways emphasize that production deployment can be achieved at zero cost by strategically using free tiers, mobile optimization is crucial for user engagement, and PWAs offer a native-like experience without app store dependencies. The complete source code and implementation details are available.

headline_marked: Mathematicians [[can't quit AI]] despite concerns over credit and obsolescence
headline: Mathematicians can't quit AI despite concerns over credit and obsolescence
summary: AI is proving too useful for mathematicians to abandon, even as they worry about its impact on their field and attribution.
details: Mathematician Tristan Buckmaster accuses OpenAI of using his work to rush a solution to the legendary Navier-Stokes problem. Despite his claims, he and other mathematicians find themselves unable to stop using AI tools like OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude for their research.

Buckmaster notes that AI companies hold a near-monopoly on these powerful tools, leaving researchers with little choice but to engage with them. He uses Codex to refine his papers and understand AI's problem-solving steps, even as he feels the technology may have unfairly benefited from his prior work.

The controversy highlights broader concerns about AI's role in mathematics. While AI can accelerate solutions to complex problems, it raises questions about the value of human contribution and the traditional peer-review process.

Andreas Thom, another mathematician, expressed surprise when OpenAI's Astra model claimed to solve a problem he had been working on for two decades. He questioned OpenAI researchers about their learning process, especially after they initially overlooked his own published work.

Thom, like Buckmaster, has used ChatGPT for assistance but was assured his interactions did not influence training data. However, he remains skeptical, believing AI makes it nearly impossible to trace contributions, potentially ending the era of clear academic attribution.

The rapid advancement of AI in mathematics prompts existential questions for researchers. Cornell mathematician Alex Townsend wonders how humans can make significant contributions when massive companies with vast resources are involved.
Townsend observes a growing trend among his colleagues to subscribe to AI services, feeling both excited by the possibilities and nervous about the future of human-led mathematical discovery.
